analysis.one_liner: Makes knowingly selling adulterated or misbranded food a crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison.
analysis.headline: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved the bill and placed it on the Senate calendar, but the full Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a new criminal penalty to federal food and drug law: anyone who knowingly adulterates or misbrands a food product, with conscious or reckless disregard for a risk of death or serious injury, could face up to 10 years in prison plus fines. A Senate committee approved it and put it on the Senate's waiting list for floor votes, but the Senate never took it up before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who gain an added deterrent against companies knowingly putting dangerous or mislabeled food on the market, and honest food producers who compete against sellers cutting corners on safety.

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates a new federal crime: knowingly violating the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act's bans on adulterating or misbranding food, with conscious or reckless disregard of a risk of death or serious bodily injury, punishable by up to 10 years in prison and fines.

The committee-approved version also extends the new 10-year felony penalty to knowing violations involving drugs, medical devices, tobacco products, cosmetics, and unsafe dietary supplements, where the violator disregarded a risk of death or serious injury.
Existing penalties under the food and drug law's general provision carry far shorter maximum prison terms, so this bill raises the stakes for the most egregious knowing violations.

analysis.who_pays: Food, drug, and supplement manufacturers and distributors whose employees knowingly violate safety rules while disregarding a risk of death or serious injury would face felony prosecution, prison, and fines.
analysis.who_pays_short: Food and drug manufacturers that violate safety law

drawbacks.text: The committee version reaches beyond food to drugs, devices, tobacco, and cosmetics, so a bill titled for food safety would expand criminal exposure across the FDA-regulated economy.

Criminal penalties only deter if prosecutors bring cases; the bill adds punishment on paper but no new inspectors or enforcement funding, so its real-world effect depends entirely on Justice Department priorities.
A good-faith objection is that felony prison terms for corporate employees can chill legitimate business decisions or be duplicative of existing misdemeanor penalties for the same conduct.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is straightforward: knowingly putting consumers at risk of death or serious injury would carry real prison time instead of a modest fine. The penalty is narrowed to knowing violations with conscious or reckless disregard, which limits the risk of punishing honest mistakes. The main limits are that the bill adds no enforcement resources and quietly broadens to non-food products.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee approved it and put it on the Senate's calendar of bills awaiting floor action, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Leahy introduced the bill on September 13, 2010, and it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
On September 23, 2010, the Judiciary Committee reported the bill favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute that replaced the original version.
The same day, the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders, the list of bills waiting for the full Senate to act.
No further action was taken; the Senate never voted on the bill, and the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that knowingly ship unsafe food, and any other FDA-regulated products covered by the committee amendment, are better off because the bill died without a Senate vote; the added felony exposure never became law.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows no votes and no recorded opposition; the bill simply never reached the Senate floor, so the partisan shape of the fight cannot be determined from the record.

industries.note: The bill would expose their employees to up to 10 years in prison for knowingly selling adulterated or misbranded food while disregarding a risk of death or serious injury. The industry's interest in avoiding felony liability runs against consumers' interest in safer food.
The committee version adds the felony penalty for knowingly introducing unsafe dietary supplements into interstate commerce, a provision aimed at a market with a history of unsafe products.

industries.industry: Drug, device, tobacco, and cosmetics makers
industries.note: The committee amendment extends the 10-year penalty beyond food to knowing safety-law violations involving these products, broadening criminal exposure across FDA-regulated industries.
